newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - Vietnam keeps budding coffee industry on the boil.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Vietnam keeps budding coffee industry on the boil.

text.p: Two years ago, Nguyen Thi Mai was full of beans.
Vietnam was producing coffee like never before, the price of the commodity was rocketing and she had earned enough to pay for a family house, a colour television and a gleaming new motorcycle.

Now, with prices languishing at around $1,250 a tonne, just 30 percent of their 1994 peak, Mai is worried that the rewards for her toil in the vast plantations of Dak Lak province will be less than instant.
"For this crop, prices will be too low," Mai said as she pruned branches laden with the green "cherries" which will be ready for picking in a few weeks' time.
"It was quite difficult for us last year. This year we will work just as hard and earn even less," she said.
Like so many in Buon Ma Thuot -- the capital of this central highlands province -- Mai has done well out of coffee.
COFFEE PRODUCERS URGED TO OPERATE STRICT EXPORT QUOTAS
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) says that to prevent boom turning to bust, coffee-growing countries should operate strict quotas on exports to force prices higher.
Hanoi, which has so far declined to join the ACPC because it cannot afford to buy and store coffee stocks, has its own answer -- grind out more beans.

Hoang Thanh Tiem, vice-director of the national Coffee Research Institute, says he expects the coming harvest to yield 270,000 tonnes, a jump of more than 17 percent from last year's crop of 230,000 tonnes.
Today, the country has around 200,000 hectares (494,000 acres) of coffee under cultivation, about 30 times more than at the end of the Vietnam War in 1975.

Desperate for the hard currency that coffee exports bring, the government wants more. It has set an area-under-cultivation target for 2005 of at least 320,000 hectares (790,700 acres) (790,000 acres).
The coffee plant was first brought to Vietnam in 1857.

For the next century several small-time plantations in the north were operated by the country's French colonial masters and then, after the Vietnam War, they struggled on with help from Soviet-bloc allies such as East Germany.
But in the late 1980s, when the communist cooperative system of agriculture broke down and Hanoi opened its doors to trade with the outside world, the coffee business really took off.
HOW VIETNAM'S COFFEE INDUSTRY HAS GROWN
Vietnam is now Asia's second-largest coffee producer after Indonesia and the world's sixth-largest exporter.
It earned an estimated $425 million from exporting about 230,000 tonnes of beans during the 1995/96 harvest, putting coffee just behind oil and rice as a source of foreign exchange.
At first glance, Buon Ma Thuot, with its red dirt-track roads, ramshackle houses and scruffy outdoor markets, may not look like a boomtown. But it is.

Nguyen Van Thuong, Director of the Viet Duc Cofexim coffee company, says that depending on crop and prices, plantation workers can earn up to $100 a month -- slightly more than the average income in old Saigon, the country's economic powerhouse.
That new wealth has filtered through to the local community.
Walk into a cafe in Buon Ma Thuot and you are likely to be served green tea, not coffee. But ask about the latest price of coffee on the London market and you are likely to get a quote.

The promise of rich pickings has drawn thousands of migrants to Dak Lak, home to 60 percent of Vietnam's coffee plantations. According to the Lao Dong newspaper, the province's population has grown to 1.5 million from 340,000 in 1975.
UGLY ENVIRONMENTAL SIDE-EFFECTS
But the rapid growth of the industry has spawned ugly environmental side-effects.

In a report sent to the daily Vietnam News earlier this year, a leading representative of ethnic minority groups and a senior government official slammed the "excessive and indiscriminate use of fertilisers and insecticides by coffee planters".
Some say that may explain Vietnam's astonishingly high yields of 1.6 tonnes per hectare, much higher than a typical yield of 0.6 tonnes in other coffee-producing countries.

The two critics said that heavy use of fertilisers, illegal destruction of the highlands' tropical forests and over-use of subterranean water resources are a serious threat to both biodiversity and the downstream rice-growing belt.

"Some environmentalists even predict the red-soil plateaux and mountains of the region could become a vast desert...with natural disasters in the last few years already indicating how the biodiversity of the region has been unbalanced," they said.
Of more immediate concern to the industry is Vietnam's reputation for inconsistent quality and unreliable supply.

Vietnam's farmers have earned a bad name for defaulting on contracts by witholding coffee when the market is rising in the hope of getting a higher price. With contract law ill-defined, to say the least, buyers have had little legal recourse.
Nevertheless, Viet Duc Cofexim's Thuong says defaulting has become less of a problem since 1994, when the government cut the list of authorised coffee traders to 28 from more than 100.

On quality, buyers often complain that farmers still lay beans out in the sun to dry, where they get mixed up with dirt, and that bags of coffee often come with beans of differing size and moisture content.
Anxious to improve quality, the government has encouraged foreign firms to invest in processing projects to replace antiquated plants.

It has also set its sights on bumping up output of arabica coffee, a more precious variety used in gourmet brews and usually grown in South America. At present, 95 percent of Vietnam's output is robusta, which is used for instant coffee.
Quality coffee may interest connoisseurs overseas, but for most Vietnamese...well, it's just not their cup of tea.
"I like selling coffee, not drinking it," says Van Thanh Huy of the import-export company, Inexim Daklak. "I prefer tea."
